title: What a Small Business Website Needs Before It Brings In Calls
excerpt: What a Columbus small business website needs before it brings in calls: the first screen on a phone, a page for each service, proof you're real and a short quote form.
author: David Stein
featuredAlt: Bright office desk with a large monitor, a laptop and potted plants by tall windows
content:
Before a small business website can bring in calls, it needs to answer three questions in the first screen on a phone: what you do, where you do it, and how to reach you. That means a plain headline, your service area, and a phone number people can tap. After that comes a page for each service, real photos, and a short quote form. Everything else is extra.

I build websites for small businesses in Columbus, mostly for contractors, home service companies, dental offices and restaurants. Below is the list I check before a site goes live, in the order I'd fix things if your current site isn't getting calls.

The first screen on a phone

A lot of your visitors find you on a phone, often while standing in a kitchen with a leak or in a parking lot looking for lunch. They decide fast whether to stay. Build the top of the page for that person.

  • A headline that says what you do in plain words, like roof repair and replacement in Columbus.
  • The towns or neighborhoods you serve, near the top.
  • Your phone number, big, and set up so a tap starts the call.
  • One button for the next step: call, or request a quote.

Then check the site on your own phone. If you have to pinch, zoom or scroll to find the number, your customers do too. If the page takes a while to show anything, a lot of them won't wait.

A page for each service

One page that lists every service in a long paragraph doesn't help a customer or Google. Someone searching for gutter repair wants to land on a page about gutter repair. Give each main service its own page with:

  • What the job is and who it's for, in the words a customer would use.
  • The areas you cover for that service.
  • Photos of that kind of work.
  • Answers to the questions people ask you on the phone.
  • The same call button and quote form as the home page.

Service pages also help with local search. Google reads them to understand what you do, and they give your local SEO something to work with. The map listing still depends on your Google Business Profile and reviews, which I covered in a plain checklist for Google Maps.

Proof that you're real

People call the business that looks established and nearby. You don't need a big brand to look that way. You need a few honest signals.

  • Real photos of your trucks, your crew, your office and your finished work. Stock photos read as stock.
  • Your name, address and phone number in the footer, matching your Google listing.
  • Reviews or quotes from customers, with their permission.
  • Licenses or memberships you actually hold, if your trade has them.

Leave out anything you can't back up. A claim of being the top company in town or a big made-up number does more harm than good when a customer checks.

A quote form people finish

Some people won't call. They'd rather type a few lines at night and hear back in the morning. Give them a form, and keep it short: name, phone or email, what they need and where. Ask for the rest when you call them back.

Make sure the form actually reaches you. Send yourself a test after any change to the site, and check that the email doesn't land in spam. A form that quietly fails is worse than no form, because the customer thinks they reached you.

If you run ads, mail postcards or put a QR code on a yard sign, send those people to a page made for that offer instead of the home page. A landing page that matches the EDDM postcard they just got makes the next step obvious.

Make it match the rest of your brand

Your trucks, signs, cards and website all tell people who you are. When the colors and logo don't match, it looks like two different companies. When they do, you look like a business that's been around. Because I also handle print, signs and vehicle graphics, I build the site from the same logo, colors and fonts.

The rest is upkeep. Update your hours before holidays, swap in new photos when you finish a good job, and fix a broken link when you find one. A site that looks cared for gets more calls than one that looks abandoned. For what a site should say in your trade, see marketing for roofing companies and marketing for dental offices.

Not sure where your site stands?

Open your website on your phone and pretend you're a customer who has never heard of you. Can you tell what you do, where you work and how to call within a few seconds? If not, start there.
